captions.text: Picture the end of a meal.
At the bottom of a plate, a grain of rice, forgotten.
Nobody wants it…
and yet, there is a flame in there.
Let us follow it.
Here it is in the scrap caddy, with the day’s leftovers.
On a bench, with no ceremony at all, it is drowned in a bucket of water, up to the ten-litre mark.
It dives into a funnel, and a long pipe carries it off,
right to the bottom of a black tank, without a bubble of air.
Let us go in with it, into one single drop.
Tiny creatures cut it up, and others turn it into acids.
And the last of them, slow and fragile, turn it into methane.
There: our grain of rice has become a bubble!
Up it comes, and slips under another tank, turned over, which floats and rises with the gas.
Come evening, the gas leaves through a hose, pushed by next to nothing: two centimetres of water.
And under a pot, when the time comes, a small blue flame you can hardly see.
What is left in the tank is not lost: it goes back to the vegetable bed.
That is the whole story: a grain of rice, a drop, a bubble, a bell…
and a tenth of a second of flame.
A few landmarks: four views, the yard, the tank, the drop and the gas line.
Click a part: its sheet opens, and you can hear its story.
One guide tells how the two tanks go together, another runs from the plot to the daily feed.
The simulation changes the meal, the place, the month, and runs twelve scenarios.
Seven lessons, with quizzes, explain the life of the tank.
Ten sheets gather the drawings.
One last thing: this lab is an educational reconstruction.
It follows a real plant, from a thesis: just one, four months, at Dar es Salaam.
It is neither a plan to follow nor a product of its designers.
It proves nothing about the safety of a plant in your home.
And before you build anything, ask your local authority.
The figures come from the thesis and other documents, or from our simulation and our estimates.
The Sources panel says who said what.
That leaves the winter at Geneva: does a bare tank last it?
Our model cannot decide.
It all rests on one figure, the activation energy.
And we found no measurement of a plant of this kind below about twenty-five degrees.
The scenario A winter at Geneva puts that slider in your hands.
Come on, the meal is over, and our grain of rice is waiting for you!

segments.title: From kitchen scraps to a flame

captions.text: A yard, in a warm climate, and the whole circle at a glance.
The scrap caddy: that is where our grain of rice waits.
The plant: two water tanks, one turned over inside the other.
The gas leaves by this hose, across the yard, to the kitchen, only a few metres away.
What goes into the tank pushes as much into this bucket, and the bucket ends at the bed: the circle is shut.
And this tree?
At Dar es Salaam three were cut down, because a black tank wants the sun.
In the simulation, the sun and the figures follow the place.
This yard does not change: its mango trees do not show Geneva.
And if night falls while we talk, that is normal: days are very short here.

segments.title: Two tanks, a bell that rises

captions.text: The machine alone, and it opens already cut.

Its true speed, about fifty centimetres a day, would not show.
And whatever size you choose in the simulation, this view stays that of the thousand-litre tank.

segments.title: One drop, and what lives in it

captions.text: The real machine is alive.

On the left, all that remains of our grain of rice.
